title: The whole church in one man
sum: Ignatius greets 'the holy church that is in Tralles in Asia', at peace through Christ's suffering, 'in the fullness, in the apostolic manner' (1:0). Its overseer Polybius came to him at Smyrna and showed him a church blameless and unwavering 'not as a habit but by nature'; in Polybius he saw the whole congregation (1:1). Through him Ignatius received their goodwill and found them 'imitators of God' (1:2).

views.H: Tralles, on the road east from Magnesia, sent only its overseer (Lightfoot). Eusebius names him as the church's 'ruler then' (Church History 3.36.5).
views.N: 'Christ Jesus our hope' (1 Timothy 1:1); 'imitators of God' (Ephesians 5:1).

settings.what: The greeting and thanks for Polybius
settings.to: The church at Tralles in the Roman province of Asia, whose overseer Polybius had visited Ignatius
settings.when: Under guard at Smyrna, on the way to Rome
settings.why: To thank the church for sending its overseer, and to praise it before the warnings that follow. Lake: each letter but Romans is first a thank-you 'for the kindness which they had shown to Ignatius'.
settings.readers: The Trallian Christians who heard it read, with Polybius back among them; Lightfoot notes that the letter is the earliest notice of a church at Tralles at all.

title: Deacons of the mysteries
sum: When they are subject to the overseer as to Jesus Christ, they live not in a human way but in Christ's, who died for them (2:1). So they must do nothing without the overseer, and be subject to the council of elders 'as to the apostles of Jesus Christ' (2:2). The deacons are 'deacons of the mysteries of Jesus Christ', 'not deacons of food and drink, but assistants of the church of God', and must guard against blame 'as they would against fire' (2:3).
readings: Lightfoot: 2:3 is 'not an injunction of obedience due to the deacons ... but a statement of requirements from them'; 'Not their claims, but their duties, are enforced.' Catholic teaching quotes the next verse for the three degrees of orders (Catechism 1554).
Lightfoot: a word against a lowly view of deacons

In Acts the Seven are chosen so that the Twelve need not set aside the word of God 'to serve tables' (Acts 6:2). Lightfoot: such duties 'tended to engross the interests of the deacon', who 'needed therefore to be reminded that the diaconate had a higher aspect also'. The card at Acts 6 asks whether the Seven were deacons at all.

views.N: Lake's margin gives 1 Corinthians 4:1 ('assistants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries'); Acts 6:1-6 and 1 Timothy 3:8-13 on deacons.
views.C: See the card at Acts 6 (deacons) and the cards on bishops and elders at Acts 20:28 and 1 Timothy 3.

deep.b:
Chapters 2-3 give the fullest list in the letters: the overseer is to be obeyed 'as Jesus Christ' (2:1) and respected as 'a type of the Father' (3:1); the elders are 'the apostles of Jesus Christ' (2:2), 'God's council' and 'the band of the apostles' (3:1); the deacons are respected 'as Jesus Christ' (3:1). In Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1 the pictures shift: the overseer 'in the place of God', the deacons with 'the ministry of Jesus Christ'. Ignatius is not drawing a fixed chart; he uses the strongest images he has for a church that holds together.

Lightfoot summed up the pattern in The Christian Ministry: 'If the bishop occupies the place of God or of Jesus Christ, the presbyters are as the Apostles, as the council of God', and he called it 'this extravagant exaltation of the episcopal office', while noting that 'the presbyters are not put out of sight'.

settings.what: On the overseer, the elders and the deacons
settings.to: The Trallian church, already living in this order ('as you already do', 2:2)
settings.why: To confirm the church in its order and to raise the standing of its deacons, before the warning against false teaching (6-11), for which this order is the guard.
settings.readers: A church Ignatius praises as already subject to its overseer; Lake's introduction counts strengthening 'respect for the bishop and presbyters' among the aims of every letter.

title: Without these it is not called a church
sum: Let everyone respect the deacons as Jesus Christ, the overseer as 'a type of the Father', and the elders as 'God's council and as the band of the apostles'. 'Without these, it is not called a church' (3:1). Ignatius has the model of their love in their overseer, whose bearing is 'a great lesson' and whose gentleness 'is power' (3:2). He could write more sharply, but he will not give orders 'like an apostle' (3:3).
readings: The Catechism: a definition of the church
No church without overseer, elders and deacons. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes the verse in full (Catechism 1554).
Lightfoot: a title the church must deserve

Lightfoot paraphrases: 'Without these three orders no church has a title to the name, deserves to be called a church', reading ou kaleitai as 'is not recognised'. In The Christian Ministry he weighs the letters' language as 'extravagant' (see the views note).

views.H: Lightfoot wrote that the letters' language, 'if taken literally', would give the bishop's office 'the crushing despotism', and set beside it 'the extenuating fact, that the needs and distractions of the age seemed to call for a greater concentration of authority in the episcopate'. At 3:1 the Greek manuscript reads 'Son of the Father' for 'type of the Father'; 3:3 is corrupt in all the witnesses (Lake). See the variants.
views.N: The New Testament knows overseers and deacons (Philippians 1:1) and elders called overseers (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5-7), but no sentence like this one.
views.C: The views note at 3:1 gives each church's reading; see also the Ephesians book card 'What is the church' and the cards at Acts 20:28 and 1 Timothy 3.

deep.h: 'Without these it is not called a church'
deep.b: Greek chōris toutōn ekklēsia ou kaleitai, word for word 'apart from these a church is not called'. Lake: 'Without these the name of "Church" is not given.' The Catechism's English: 'For without them one cannot speak of the Church' (Catechism 1554). The sentence is about naming: a gathering without these offices does not, for Ignatius, bear the name church. Fritz Guy notes the wordplay of this verse: ekklēsia means 'called out', and the 'church' is 'not called'.

Lake: 'The text is here confused and corrupt in all the authorities.' The Greek manuscript's words, as Lightfoot gives them, hardly make sense; the Armenian and the long recension agree on 'Because I love you' and 'more sharply' (Lightfoot), and Lake prints the sentence mended on those lines, with a 'not' that is not in the Greek manuscript and has no note; Lightfoot adds words of his own conjecture to complete the next clause ('but I did not think myself fit for this'). The thought is clear either way: Ignatius, 'a condemned man', will not command like an apostle (Ignatius to the Romans 4:3). See the variant.

echoes: Philippians 1:1; Acts 20:28; Titus 1:5-7; 2 Corinthians 10:1; Ephesians 2:12; Ignatius to the Romans 4:3

settings.what: On respect for the three offices, and Polybius's example
settings.why: To give the order its strongest form, and then to soften it: the overseer's gentleness is power, and Ignatius will not command.
settings.readers: The Trallians, to whom Ignatius holds up their own overseer's 'very bearing' as 'a great lesson' (3:2); Lightfoot cites these chapters among the letters' strongest words on the episcopate.

title: Afraid of praise
sum: Ignatius has 'many thoughts in God' but takes his own measure, for fear of perishing by boasting; those who praise him are 'whipping' him (4:1). He loves to suffer but does not know if he is worthy; 'the jealousy' fights him unseen, so he needs gentleness, by which 'the ruler of this age is brought down' (4:2).

views.N: Paul's thorn in the flesh 'to keep me from lifting myself too high' (2 Corinthians 12:7); 'rulers of this age' (1 Corinthians 2:6).
views.H: Lake reads 'the jealousy of the devil', with 'ambition' as a second possibility (see the note).

echoes: 2 Corinthians 12:7; 1 Corinthians 2:6; Ignatius to the Romans 5:3

settings.when: Between the call to order and the warning
settings.why: To show in his own case the humility he asks of them, and to explain why he does not write of 'heavenly things'.
settings.readers: Readers who would soon hear him warn others against being 'puffed up' (7:1) heard him admit the danger first.

title: Heavenly things for infants
sum: Ignatius could write of heavenly things, but fears to harm them, 'since you are infants' (5:1). He himself understands 'the places of the angels and the gatherings of the rulers, seen and unseen', yet that does not make him a disciple: 'much is still lacking in us, so that we may not lack God' (5:2).

views.N: 1 Corinthians 3:1-2 (milk for 'infants in Christ'); Colossians 1:16 ('the seen and the unseen'), in Lake's margin; 1 Corinthians 8:1 ('Knowledge puffs up').
views.H: Lake's margin reference at 5:1 is read '3, 1. 2' in one scan of his page and '8, 1. 2' in the other; 1 Corinthians 3:1-2 is the passage on infants.

title: Poison in honeyed wine
sum: Ignatius urges them, 'not I but the love of Jesus Christ', to eat only Christian food and keep away from 'the foreign weed, which is heresy' (6:1). The false teachers mix Jesus Christ into their teaching to win trust, like poisoners who hide a deadly drug in honeyed wine, which the unsuspecting drinks gladly 'and with evil pleasure takes his death' (6:2).
Lake calls 6:2 'clearly corrupt'; Lightfoot mends it to 'they even mingle poison with Jesus Christ'.

views.H: The letter does not name the teachers. Lake's introduction calls their teaching 'docetism'; Lightfoot: 'The main purport of the letter is a warning against the poison of Docetism (§§ 6-11)'.
views.N: Romans 16:18 ('smooth words and flattering talk'); Matthew 15:13 (the plant not planted by the Father, at 11:1).

settings.to: The Trallian church, warned in advance
settings.why: To keep the church from teachers who sound Christian but empty Christ's suffering of reality, and to bind it to the overseer, elders and deacons as the guard (7:2).
settings.readers: A church Ignatius says is not yet touched ('It is not that I know of anything of this kind among you', 8:1); Lightfoot: 'He acquits the Trallians indeed of any complicity in this heresy hitherto'.

title: Within the altar
sum: Guard against such people: be humble, and stay 'inseparable from God Jesus Christ, and from the overseer and the ordinances of the apostles' (7:1). 'Whoever is within the altar is pure, but whoever is outside the altar is not pure': whoever acts without the overseer, the elders and the deacons 'is not pure in his conscience' (7:2).

views.N: Hebrews 13:10 ('We have an altar'); 2 Thessalonians 2:15 (the apostles' traditions).
views.C: To be 'within the altar' is, as Ignatius explains, to act with the overseer, elders and deacons. Christ's presence in the Supper and whether it is a sacrifice are the cards at Matthew 26:26 and Hebrews 10.

echoes: Hebrews 13:10; 2 Thessalonians 2:15; Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:2; Ignatius to the Magnesians 7:2

title: Faith the flesh, love the blood
sum: Ignatius does not know of anything like this among them, but warns them in advance against 'the snares of the devil'. Let them take up a gentle spirit and recover their strength in faith, 'which is the flesh of the Lord', and in love, 'which is the blood of Jesus Christ' (8:1). Let no one hold a grudge, and give the Gentiles no excuse to insult God's people: 'Woe to the one through whom my name is insulted for no reason among some' (8:2).

views.N: Isaiah 52:5 and Romans 2:24 stand behind 8:2 (Lake's margin); the wording is Ignatius's own (see the note).
views.H: Lightfoot counts 8:2 among the three formal quotations of the Old Testament in the seven letters.

title: Truly born, truly crucified, truly raised
sum: 'So be deaf when anyone speaks to you apart from Jesus Christ.' He was of David's family and of Mary, 'truly born', he ate and drank, he was 'truly persecuted under Pontius Pilate', 'truly crucified and died, in the sight of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth' (9:1). He was 'also truly raised from the dead' by his Father, who will raise believers in the same way; without him 'we do not have true life' (9:2).
Four times in two verses Ignatius says 'truly', against those who said Christ's life and suffering were only an appearance (10:1).

views.H: Lightfoot: 'The denunciation of Docetism is fuller and more explicit in this than in any other of his letters'; his paraphrase: 'His human body was no mere phantom. He was really born. He really ate and drank.' The letter does not name the teachers or say whether they also kept Jewish practices (Lake: 'it is disputed'). Lake's margin sets Paul's argument of 1 Corinthians 15:12-20 beside 9:2.
views.N: Romans 1:3 (David's offspring), Galatians 4:4 ('born of a woman'), Acts 10:41 (eating and drinking), 1 Timothy 6:13 (Pilate), Philippians 2:10 (heaven, earth, under the earth), 1 Corinthians 15:12-20 (raised), 1 John 4:2-3 and 2 John 1:7 (come in the flesh).
views.C: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1-2 and Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2 have similar lists. Whether 'under the earth' bears on Christ's descent to the dead is taken up in the topic The Descent into Hades.

deep.b: The Greek runs as a chain of clauses hung on 'Jesus Christ': tou ek genous Daueid, tou ek Marias, hos alēthōs egennēthē, ephagen te kai epien, alēthōs ediōchthē epi Pontiou Pilatou, alēthōs estaurōthē kai apethanen ... hos kai alēthōs ēgerthē apo nekrōn. The Plain English Translation breaks it into sentences but keeps every 'truly'. 'Of Mary' (not 'of a virgin') and 'ate and drank' are both aimed at the reality of his body. 'In the sight of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth' borrows Philippians 2:10 to make all creation a witness.

Lake's introduction: 'docetism (δοκεῖν), which regarded the sufferings, and in some cases the life, of Jesus as merely an appearance'. In 10:1 Ignatius quotes the claim, 'he suffered only in appearance', and turns it back: 'they themselves are only in appearance!' His answer is the same as John's: 'any spirit that confesses Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is from God' (1 John 4:2). See the topic Docetism.

echoes: Romans 1:3; Galatians 4:4; Acts 10:41; 1 Timothy 6:13; Philippians 2:10; 1 Corinthians 15:12-20; 1 John 4:2-3; 2 John 1:7; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1-2

settings.what: The confession of the true Christ, against docetism
settings.when: At the center of the warning against heresy
settings.why: To give the church the facts of Christ's life and death, each marked 'truly', so that the teachers' Christ, who only seemed to suffer, is seen as no Christ at all; and to argue from Ignatius's own chains (10:1).
settings.readers: Christians in Tralles, a city on the main road east from Ephesus (Lightfoot); Ignatius has heard of no one among them who holds the teaching (8:1). Lightfoot: Tralles lay 'in a district where Jews abounded', and a document in Josephus (Antiquities 14.10.20) is 'satisfactory evidence of their presence in Tralles in considerable numbers before the age of Ignatius'; he thinks they 'would act as a conductor to this heretical teaching'.
views: Lightfoot: a comparison with the other letters shows 'these false teachers to have been Judaizers also'.
Lake: whether the Judaizing tendency belonged to docetic circles 'is disputed'.

title: Then I die for nothing
sum: If, as some godless people say, Christ 'suffered only in appearance' (and 'they themselves are only in appearance!'), why is Ignatius in chains? Why does he pray to fight wild beasts? 'Then I am dying for nothing. Then I am telling lies about the Lord' (10:1).

views.N: Paul argues the same way: 'why are we in danger every hour?' and 'I fought with wild beasts at Ephesus' (1 Corinthians 15:30-32).
views.H: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 4:2 repeats the argument from his chains.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 15:30-32; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 4:2

title: Branches of the cross
sum: Run from 'the bad offshoots that bear deadly fruit'; whoever tastes it dies. 'These people are not the Father's planting' (11:1). If they were, they would be branches of the cross, with fruit that does not decay. By the cross Christ calls his members, for 'a head cannot be born apart, without members, since God promises union, which is himself' (11:2).

views.N: Matthew 15:13 (Lake's margin), John 15:5 (vine and branches), Colossians 1:18 and 1 Corinthians 12:12 (head and body).
views.C: The church as Christ's body is the card 'What is the church' in Ephesians.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the two trees of Eden
deep.b: Ignatius sets two plants side by side: the false teachers' offshoots with 'deadly fruit' that kills whoever tastes it (11:1), and the cross whose branches bear 'incorruptible' fruit (11:2). Lightfoot's note on 'incorruptible' already makes the link to Eden's tree: 'For the Cross is the true ξύλον ζωῆς' ('tree of life'). I suggest the pair goes further and recalls both trees of Eden: one tree's fruit brought death (Genesis 2:17; 3:6) and the tree of life stood beside it (Genesis 2:9; compare Revelation 22:2). On this reading the heresy is the forbidden tree as well as the cross the tree of life. Ignatius does not name Eden.
deep.refs: 11:1-2; Genesis 2:9; Genesis 2:17; Revelation 22:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:2

echoes: Matthew 15:13; Matthew 7:17; John 15:5; Colossians 1:18; Romans 12:5; 1 Corinthians 12:12; Acts 5:30

title: My chains urge you
sum: Ignatius greets them from Smyrna with the churches there, who have refreshed him (12:1). His chains urge them on: let them stay in harmony and prayer, and let each, above all the elders, refresh the overseer (12:2). Let them listen in love, so that the letter is not a witness against them, and pray for him, that he may reach his lot and 'not be found disqualified' (12:3).

views.H: At 12:2 the Greek manuscript's wording may mean 'the Father of Jesus Christ' (Lightfoot). At 12:3 Lightfoot calls the verb 'obviously corrupt' and prints Bunsen's emendation (see the variants).

settings.to: The Trallian church, and in it its elders
settings.when: At Smyrna, with the delegates of other churches present
settings.why: To close with the bonds that tie the churches together: greetings, prayer for Ignatius and for Syria, and a last call to obey the overseer and love one another.
settings.readers: Elders who were singled out ('above all for the elders') to care for their overseer; the whole church, asked to pray for Ignatius (12:3) and for the church in Syria (13:1).

title: My spirit an offering for you
sum: The love of the Smyrnaeans and Ephesians greets them. Let them pray for the church in Syria, whose least member Ignatius is (13:1). 'Farewell in Jesus Christ': let them be subject to the overseer and the elders and love one another 'with an undivided heart' (13:2). His spirit 'gives itself as an offering' for them, now and when he reaches God; he is still in danger, but the Father is faithful (13:3).

views.N: 1 Corinthians 15:9 ('the least of the apostles'); 2 Timothy 4:6 ('a drink offering being poured out').
views.H: The church in Syria is Antioch; from Troas Ignatius later writes that it is at peace (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2).

echoes: 1 Corinthians 15:9; 2 Timothy 4:6; Philippians 2:17; Ignatius to the Ephesians 8:1
